justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 85.9 for the one-day horizon and rising gradually to 87.5 at one month. The one-day estimate is anchored primarily by recent price action, momentum indicators, and short-term mean-reversion tendencies — essentially, I'm assuming that whatever the asset was trading at recently will persist with only minor drift. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive trend assumption, perhaps supported by broader market conditions or sector tailwinds that I was weighing at the time. The one-month estimate continues that gentle upward trajectory, incorporating a longer-run expected return or fundamental drift that compounds over a four-week window. In all three cases, the point estimates are relatively close together, suggesting I did not anticipate a dramatic directional move — just a slow, steady grind higher.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which is entirely expected given how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units (83.2 to 88.6), reflecting the relatively tight band of outcomes that can plausibly occur within a single trading session. By one week, that band widens to 12 units, capturing the broader range of news, sentiment shifts, and macro developments that could materialize over several days. At one month, the interval stretches to 25 units — nearly the full width from 75 to 100 — reflecting the deeply uncertain nature of medium-term price forecasting, where earnings surprises, central bank decisions, geopolitical events, or liquidity shocks can all materially alter outcomes.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro conditions — an unexpected rate hike, a credit event, or a sharp risk-off move in global markets — could drive prices well below 75 at the one-month horizon. Liquidity crises or forced selling by large institutional holders could also cause sharp, discontinuous drops that my intervals don't fully capture, since I was likely modeling roughly normal return distributions. On the upside, a strong earnings beat, a surprise policy easing, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above 100. My intervals also assume no structural breaks or regime changes, meaning a fundamental shift in how the asset is valued — say, a regulatory change or a major acquisition — could easily render my entire forecast distribution obsolete.
